# Results — Study 652 (Index-Deletion-Bounce)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test — **stocks
deleted from the S&P 500 get dumped by index funds into the effective date, then rebound**
(Chen, Noronha & Singal 2004) — tested on a market-adjusted (vs SPY) cumulative abnormal
return over the [-5..+40] trading-session window around the effective date. Offline &
deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number. As-of
**2026-06-30** (the last complete calendar month; the sample's own last event is
2025-09-22). Fingerprint `374248b9d621` (SPY OHLC).*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily OHLC, per-ticker event windows (48 usable tickers) + SPY OHLC (3,643 rows), 2012-01-03 → 2026-06-30 |
| Deletion calendar | **hardcoded** table of **70 real S&P 500 deletions**, effective 2012-12-11 → 2025-09-22, all coded by S&P Dow Jones Indices as "Market capitalization change" (distress deletions — the company shrank out of the index — not an acquisition/spin-off/bankruptcy removal, whose tickers vanish outright). Source: S&P Dow Jones Indices index-news announcement PDFs, via the Wikipedia "List of S&P 500 companies" change log |
| Events | **70** hardcoded deletions; **48** have a full [-5..+40] real-tape window; **22 (31%) have NO usable tape on Yahoo at all** — see the survivorship note below |
| Statistics | One-sample *t* per event-window offset (mean CAR / SE); a percentile bootstrap CI (5,000 draws, event-level resampling); a 300-draw random-day placebo per ticker; an era-split Welch *t* of the difference |
| Execution / costs | one documented convention (third axis only): enter the deleted stock at the **effective-date close** (public days ahead via the S&P press release — zero look-ahead), hold 40 trading sessions, exit; one round trip = 2 × one-way cost × NAV; return is already market-adjusted vs SPY (excess-vs-excess by construction) |
| Data quirks (named) | basket restricted *by construction* to "market cap change" deletions — M&A/spin-off/bankruptcy deletions are excluded because the ticker disappears on the effective date and there is nothing to hold "long" into |

**Survivorship, named on the Signal axis.** Of the 70 hardcoded deletions, **22 (31%) —
`ADS`, `APOL`, `BIG`, `BTU`, `CHK`, `CMA`, `DISH`, `DNR`, `FBHS`, `FL`, `FTR`, `GPS`, `HBI`,
`JDSU`, `LM`, `MNK`, `PDCO`, `RRD`, `SRCL`, `WIN`, `WPX`, `X` — have no usable tape left on
Yahoo Finance at all**, confirmed against Yahoo's own chart endpoint. Every one of these
suffered an *unrelated, later* corporate death (bankruptcy: Frontier/`FTR`, Chesapeake/`CHK`,
Windstream/`WIN`, Mallinckrodt/`MNK`; acquisition or take-private years afterward: Comerica/
`CMA`, Dish Network/`DISH`, Fortune Brands Home & Security/`FBHS`, RR Donnelley/`RRD`, Big
Lots/`BIG`) — when that later, unrelated death happens, Yahoo drops the *entire* history,
including the untouched days around **our** 2012-2025 event. This is a real, **directional**
bias: the events that survive on the tape are disproportionately the ones whose companies did
*not* keep sinking into oblivion, which tilts the usable 48-event panel *toward* finding a
rebound relative to the true, unobservable 70-event population. Even so — see below — no
rebound is found.

## The headline — market-adjusted CAR by offset (vs SPY, around the effective date)

| offset | -5 | -3 | -1 | **0** | +1 | +5 | +10 | +20 | +30 | +40 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| mean CAR | -0.59% | -0.34% | -1.05% | **-0.99%** | -1.03% | -1.56% | -1.40% | -3.11% | -4.00% | -0.94% |
| one-sample *t* | -2.08 | -0.54 | -1.44 | **-1.41** | -1.22 | -1.44 | -0.92 | -1.68 | -2.01 | -0.45 |

n = 48 real events at every offset (only tickers with a complete [-5..+40] window are kept).

- **The dump [-5..0]:** mean **-0.99%**, one-sample *t* = **-1.41**, 95% bootstrap CI
  **[-2.34%, +0.40%]** — negative, as expected, but **does not clear the *t* ≥ 2 bar** and the
  CI straddles zero. The forced-selling dump CNS document is at best a faint shrug here.
- **The rebound [+1..+40]:** mean **+0.05%**, one-sample *t* = **+0.02**, 95% bootstrap CI
  **[-4.31%, +4.47%]** — statistically indistinguishable from **exactly zero**. There is no
  rebound to certify. If anything, CAR drifts *further negative* through the middle of the
  window (offset +30: -4.00%, *t* = -2.01) before partially recovering by offset +40 — the
  opposite of a clean reversal, more like noisy continued underperformance that happens to
  land back near zero by day 40.
- **Announce → effective CAR** (the informed-selling leg, mirroring
  [249-index-inclusion](../249-index-inclusion/)'s ADD-side identity): mean **-1.21%**,
  *t* = **-1.36** (n = 47) — again negative, again short of the bar.

## Random-day placebo — a real but secondary finding, explicitly NOT promoted to the headline

For each of the 48 tickers, we drew a random non-event anchor day from **its own** trading
history (excluding a buffer around the true event) and ran the identical [+1..+40] CAR
machinery, 300 times.

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| observed post-event [+1..+40] mean CAR | **+0.05%** |
| random-day placebo mean (sd) | **-6.20%** (2.72%), 300 draws |
| *p*-value (placebo ≥ observed) | **0.010** |

Read literally, the post-effective window is *unusually good* relative to a typical 40-day
stretch for these same distressed names — because the placebo pool includes long stretches of
the pre-deletion decline (the company shrinking toward removal) and post-window continued
distress, both of which average far worse than flat. **This is a real, secondary observation
— relative stabilization around the event, not an absolute positive rebound — and it is
deliberately not used to inflate the Signal stamp**: the primary, pre-registered test is the
absolute CAR against zero (the CNS claim, "deleted stocks rebound"), and that test is a clean
miss (*t* = +0.02). A stock merely declining *less badly* than its own worst stretches is not
the same claim as "deleted stocks bounce back."

## Era contrast — first half vs second half of the 2012-2025 sample (split 2019-01-01)

CNS's own claim was that, unlike inclusion, the deletion effect had **not** decayed. This is
the within-sample test of that claim on our tape.

| era | post-event CAR [+1..+40] | n | within-era *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 2012 → 2019-01-01 | +3.21% | 11 | +0.65 |
| 2019-01-01 → 2025 | -0.88% | 37 | -0.35 |
| Welch *t* of the difference (late - early) | | | -0.74 |

Neither half shows a rebound. There is no decay to find because there was nothing alive at
the start of our sample to decay *from* — the earliest observation is already 2012, more than
a decade after CNS's original sample ends, and by then any deletion price-pressure premium
looks to have already been arbitraged flat (consistent with Petajisto 2011's broader finding
that the S&P 500 rebalance-day "index premium" has shrunk as more capital chased it).

## Third axis — the long-the-deleted timer, with costs

Enter at the effective-date close (public days ahead — zero look-ahead), hold 40 trading
sessions, exit; return is already market-adjusted vs SPY.

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| gross per event | **+0.05%** |
| net per event (5 / 10 bps one-way) | **-0.05% / -0.15%** |
| *t* (net, 5 bps) | **-0.02** |
| hit rate | 54.2% |
| worst single event | **-38.4%** |
| best single event | +46.3% |
| n | 48 |

Even at face value the point estimate is a coin flip that costs eat outright — and the tail is
brutal: a -38% single-event loss against a +46% best case, on names whose basket already lost
31% of its members to total data disappearance from a *later* corporate death. There is
nothing here that survives being turned into a real position.

## Synthetic positive control — the machinery is unbiased

Deterministic mean-reverting "distressed stock vs market" process with a TUNABLE planted
dump-then-rebound; no network.

| world | dump *t* | rebound *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| null (dump=rebound=0), **20 seeds** | mean **+0.26** (sd 0.95), \|*t*\|≥2 in **0/20** | mean **-0.30** (sd 1.02), \|*t*\|≥2 in **1/20** |
| planted dump=-8%, rebound=+8% (seed 652) | **-13.45** | **+4.74** |

The detector does not fire spuriously on the null (the one 1/20 rebound hit is within the
expected ~5% false-positive rate of a *t* = 2 threshold) and lights up cleanly on a planted
effect of realistic size. *(A faithful-engine / power check only — never cited in support of
the real-tape stamp.)*

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The dump [-5..0] is -0.99% (*t* = -1.41) and the rebound [+1..+40] is
  +0.05% (*t* = +0.02, CI straddling zero) — neither clears **t ≥ 2** on the real tape. Both
  halves of the 2012-2025 sample independently fail to show a rebound (early *t* = +0.65,
  n=11; late *t* = -0.35, n=37). The random-day placebo shows a real but secondary
  *relative-stabilization* effect (p = 0.010) that is explicitly not enough to certify the
  primary, absolute claim. **Named:** the surviving 48-event panel is tilted toward finding a
  rebound by a 31% survivorship gap (companies that later vanished from Yahoo are the ones
  most likely to have kept declining) — and even with that tailwind, nothing shows up.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** A long-the-deleted timer nets essentially zero to slightly
  negative after costs (*t* = -0.02 at 5 bps), with a -38% single-event tail. There is no
  edge to harvest even before considering that a third of the basket disappeared from
  history entirely.
- **"Has the deletion bounce escaped inclusion's fate (CNS 2004's asymmetry claim)?" —
  BUSTED.** CNS argued deletion, unlike inclusion, does not decay. On this fresh tape it is
  not alive to decay from — and sibling [249-index-inclusion](../249-index-inclusion/)
  already found the ADD-side pop dead too (ex-outlier, *t* ≈ 0). Both halves of the classic
  addition/deletion asymmetry have gone quiet.
